name: Junagadh, 1947–48
summary: The Muslim Nawab of Hindu-majority Junagadh acceded to Pakistan. India blockaded the Kathiawar enclave; the Nawab fled; Indian troops entered on 9 November 1947; a February 1948 plebiscite reported almost the entire vote for India. Pakistan’s claim remains on paper.
scaleRationale: A short integration crisis with a blockade and a token force, not a Hyderabad-scale war.

start.note: Accession announced around 15 August; Pakistan accepted 13 September.

parties.note: Accepted the accession; never sent a relieving force.

historiography.claim: India: the Nawab’s accession ignored geography and a Hindu majority; the Dewan invited Delhi in to stop administrative collapse; the plebiscite settled it.
historiography.heldBy: V.P. Menon; Government of India White Paper on Indian States

historiography.claim: Pakistan: Indian troops entered a state that had legally acceded to Pakistan; the vote was held under occupation. Official Pakistani maps still mark Junagadh.
historiography.heldBy: Liaquat Ali Khan telegram, 10 November 1947; Pakistani official cartography

name: Sikkim merger, 1975
summary: India’s protectorate became the 22nd state after the army disarmed the palace guard on 9 April 1975, a referendum on 14 April abolished the Chogyal, and the 36th Amendment took effect on 16 May. Delhi calls it a merger; the last Chogyal called it annexation.
scaleRationale: A political incorporation with one named sentry dead, not an insurgency.

resources.note: Sikkim sits on the Tibet/China frontier; Nathu La is a later interstate layer.

start.note: Anti-monarchy agitation and the 1973 tripartite agreement; the armed day is April 1975.

name: Meghalaya insurgency
summary: Khasi HNLC and Garo ANVC/GNLA campaigns over indigeneity, land and a homegrown armed underground. GNLA was broken in 2018; AFSPA left the state the same year. HNLC talks remain on and off.
scaleRationale: A two-decade state insurgency. SATP-era deaths sit in the low hundreds, not a one-district riot.

resources.note: Garo Hills coal belt as extortion and recruitment country.

start.note: HNLC split from HALC. ANVC 1990s; GNLA 2009.

end.note: GNLA collapsed after Sohan D. Shira’s death; AFSPA withdrawn 31 March 2018. HNLC residual.

name: Naga–Kuki conflict, 1992–97
summary: NSCN-IM’s Nagalim claim and Kuki armed groups fought through Manipur’s hills after Moreh exploded in 1992. Villages were emptied on both sides. Kuki memory names 13 September 1993 at Joupi as Black Day.
scaleRationale: Hundreds killed, tens of thousands displaced, several hill districts — an ethnic war inside the Naga insurgency’s map.

resources.note: Nagalim vs Kuki homeland claims; Moreh trade and hill taxation.

start.note: UCDP dates the outbreak 12 May 1992 around Moreh/Chandel; some Kuki timelines start with a killing at Moreh Bazar in June.

name: Kuki–Paite clash, 1997
summary: A fight inside the Kuki-Zo world in Churachandpur: KNF cadres killed Paite villagers at Saikul on 24 June 1997, and the district burned through the year. Official Manipur figures later put 352 dead and thousands of houses gone.
scaleRationale: One district, months of village-burning, hundreds dead and more than ten thousand displaced.

resources.note: Kuki vs Zomi/Paite label, not a religious split.

name: Manipur valley insurgency
summary: Valley Meitei groups — UNLF from 1964, PLA/RPF from 1978, then PREPAK, KYKL, KCP — fought for a sovereign Manipur from Imphal and from Myanmar camps. Parallel to, not the same as, the Naga and Kuki hill wars. UNLF signed a peace deal on 29 November 2023 while the 2023 ethnic war was still burning.
scaleRationale: Decades of secessionist war in a small valley, with a long extra-judicial-killing docket, before the 2023 ethnic explosion.

time.note: UNLF–GoI agreement 29 November 2023 covers one faction; PLA and others remain. Nested under the 2023 ethnic war, not ended by it.

accords.name: UNLF–Government of India–Manipur agreement
accords.outcome: One valley group entered designated camps during the 2023 ethnic war; it did not end street fighting.
